reason: The provided sources contain dozens of cross-verified historical facts detailing Herschel's discovery, his royal naming proposal, and international pushback.
story: In 1781, German-born musician William Herschel was scanning the constellation Gemini through a homemade reflecting telescope when he spotted a faint, moving celestial object. Thinking he had found a comet, Herschel tracked its motion until calculations proved it was an undiscovered planet—the first found since antiquity. Herschel, seeking royal favor, named the world Georgium Sidus, or 'George's Star,' in honor of Britain's King George III. The king was flattered, naming Herschel his court astronomer and funding the construction of a colossal 40-foot telescope, while also awarding William's sister and observational partner, Caroline Herschel, the first state salary ever paid to a female astronomer. But astronomers across the globe flatly rejected putting the British king into the heavens, with the French calling it 'Herschel' before the astronomical community settled on the mythological name Uranus. Today, our solar system's seventh planet carries the name of a classical god instead of King George.
angle: When William Herschel discovered the seventh planet in 1781, he officially named it 'George's Star' after King George III, but rival nations refused to look up at a planet named after the British king.

claims.claim: William Herschel was born in Hanover, Germany, in 1738 and emigrated to England in 1757.
Herschel worked as a successful musician and composer before pursuing astronomy.
Herschel hand-cast and polished his own reflecting telescope mirrors out of speculum metal.
Caroline Herschel assisted her brother William by polishing telescope mirrors and logging observational data.
On March 13, 1781, Herschel detected a faint, moving object in the constellation Gemini.
Herschel initially reported his discovery as a comet rather than a new planet.
The discovery marked the first time a new planet was identified in the solar system since antiquity.
Herschel exercised his naming preference by christening the new world 'Georgium Sidus' after King George III.
Astronomers in other countries rejected naming the planet after the British monarch, opting instead for the classical name Uranus.
In 1781, Herschel was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society and awarded the Copley Medal.
King George III appointed Herschel as his royal court astronomer following the discovery.
King George III granted £4,000 toward the construction of Herschel's giant 40-foot reflecting telescope.
King George III granted Caroline Herschel a £50 annual salary, making her the first woman in England to receive a paid scientific post.
Herschel went on to discover two major moons of Uranus, Titania and Oberon.
Herschel discovered two moons of Saturn, Mimas and Enceladus.
Herschel discovered infrared radiation in 1800 using a prism and thermometers to measure heat beyond visible red light.
Herschel catalogued 2,500 non-stellar objects, compiling the core list that became the New General Catalogue.

disputed: Whether Herschel was knighted immediately after discovering Uranus: S4 states he was knighted following the 1781 discovery, but S1 notes he was made a Knight of the Royal Guelphic Order much later in 1816 and that this was not equivalent to an official British knighthood. A script should avoid claiming an immediate formal knighthood.

The sole role of the 40-foot telescope in discovering Saturn's moons: S5 notes that attributing the discoveries of Mimas and Enceladus exclusively to the 40-foot instrument is debatable because Herschel operated multiple telescopes simultaneously, whereas S1 links them directly to the 40-foot becoming operational. A script should attribute it simply as discoveries made around that time.
